lines.text: cares of everyday life. It is not work, however precious that
may be, which can give our life exhaustive significance. It is
not our everyday toil which endows the life of man with
ultimate meaning and richest content. Life receives its true
content and meaning from what is taking place in our inner
man, our souls.
Sunday should lead us to meditate on this, among other
things: what is the ultimate meaning of all our busy care and
toil? Of this bustling activity in which we all seem to be
endlessly engaged? It comes to an end of course with death,
and what final significance has our work in view of this end
to which we are moving? Have we become more mature,
more prepared for eternity? Have we won an inner peace of
soul? Can we thank God as we look back on this past week?
Have we become more cheerful and kind? Or are we only
tired and vexed? Or do we find it uncomfortable and
repugnant to examine ourselves at all? Are we seeking in
the midst of a feverish preoccupation with our work to flee
from ourselves because we know how poor and empty we
are? Yes, Sunday is intended to remind us of the fact that
we are truly weary and heavy laden however much we are
inclined to forget it. Its purpose is to draw our attention to
those hidden things of the spirit which we most sorely need.
"The kingdom of God is not eating and drinking"
, says Paul
(neither is it toil and care), "but righteousness and peace and
joy in the Holy Ghost."
"Come to me!" thus the peal of church bells on Sunday
invites us. They call us to enter the house of God, and to
surrender ourselves to the sway of God's word. If we do that,
our Sunday will be rich in blessing, a real Day of the Lord.
"Come to me!"—to the word of God which calls us away
from our work with its thoughts and plans, its joys and
sorrows, its successes and failures, to the silence of medita-
tion; to serious and joyful self-recollection in the presence of
God; to the sense of God's glory which shines forth on us
in the face of Jesus Christ. Thus Sunday will always be for
us a new beginning, so that, after feeling "power from on
